planting.note: Plant the large bulb with its shoulder at or just above soil level in late summer to fall; it is dormant and leafless at planting time and the flower spike, not the leaves, is often the first growth to appear.

directions: This massive Mediterranean coastal bulb, also sold as Urginea maritima, produces a rosette of broad, strap-like leaves that grow through the cool, rainy winter and spring and then die back completely for a long, bone-dry summer dormancy. In late summer, before any new leaves appear, the bare bulb sends up a tall, leafless flower spike several feet high topped with a dense raceme of small, star-shaped white flowers with a faint pink midrib. Give it a hot, sharply drained, sunny site such as a rocky bank or gravel garden, since the bulb is prone to rot if kept wet during its summer rest. Established bulbs grow enormous over time and are essentially maintenance-free once planted in the right spot.

planting.note: Unlike the winter-growing Cape bulbs, this species starts active growth with warm-season rain, so plant bulbs in spring and keep them dry over winter dormancy instead of summer.

directions: Drimia elata is a South African relative of the Mediterranean sea squill, but it follows the opposite calendar from most of the Cape winter bulbs covered elsewhere in this dataset, growing and flowering during the warmer months rather than in winter. Found naturally from Namaqualand to the Cape Peninsula in grassland and sandy or clay soils, it sends up an erect to spreading raceme crowded with small purplish-brown, greenish, or whitish flowers in summer to autumn. The strap-like leaves follow or accompany flowering and die back for a dry winter rest, so water should be withheld once foliage yellows and resumed again as temperatures warm the following spring. Grow it in full sun in sharply drained soil and treat it as a dry-winter-dormant geophyte rather than the usual dry-summer pattern of its Western Cape relatives.

common_name: Kukumakranka (Cape Crocus with Fragrant Edible Fruit)

planting.note: Plant the deep-seated bulb in fall with the neck near the soil surface; leaves grow through the cool winter months and die back as the crocus-like flowers appear the following summer.

directions: Kukumakranka is a curious Western Cape geophyte that produces a tuft of narrow, spirally twisted leaves through the winter growing season; these wither away by the time the fragrant, crocus-like white flowers with pink-tinged reverse petals open directly from the bulb neck in summer. After flowering, the bulb slowly develops a club-shaped, fleshy, yellow-to-red fruit that ripens by early winter and is prized for its intense sweet fragrance, traditionally used in the Cape to flavor brandy and scent linen cupboards. It needs deep, sharply drained sandy soil and a position where it can be left entirely undisturbed for years, since it resents transplanting and is slow to re-establish. This is a true specialist-collector plant grown from seed by Southern African bulb specialists rather than a readily available garden-center item.

planting.note: Plant the small bulb shallowly in fall in a lean, clay-leaning, well-drained mix; it is a strict winter grower that must dry out completely over summer.

directions: This miniature Karoo bulb forms a pair of flat, spreading, prostrate leaves pressed almost directly against the ground, with no visible stem, making it look like a small green rosette emerging from the clay flats of its native Roggeveld. In spring it produces a dense, condensed head of red or golden-yellow tubular flowers, each with one outer petal enlarged into a showy flag, rising barely above the leaves and attracting the monkey beetles that pollinate it in the wild. It is naturally restricted to dolerite clay flats in the winter-rainfall Karoo and is considered endangered due to habitat loss, so cultivated stock from specialist bulb growers should always be preferred over wild-collected material. Because seedlings grow very slowly, taking several years to reach flowering size, it is usually grown in a bulb frame or alpine pot where its need for a bone-dry summer rest and sharp winter drainage can be carefully controlled.
